title: Smart Spending
description: Get more for every dollar: unit prices, sale tricks, impulse buys.
wolfLine: A sale is only a deal if you were going to buy it anyway.

unit-price.definition: The price for one unit (an ounce, a pound, a roll), so you can compare packs of different sizes.
unit-price.example: A 24 oz jar for $4.80 is $0.20 an ounce.

cost-per-use.definition: The price divided by how many times you’ll use something.
cost-per-use.example: $120 boots worn 300 times cost $0.40 a wear.

anchor-price.definition: A big “was” price shown next to a sale price, so the sale price feels like a steal.

impulse-buy.definition: Something you buy on the spot, unplanned, because it grabbed you in the moment.
impulse-buy.example: Candy at the checkout that wasn’t on your list.

opportunity-cost.definition: What you give up when you choose one thing over another.
opportunity-cost.example: Spend $60 on a game, and that $60 can’t go into savings.

refurbished.definition: Returned or used, then checked and repaired by the seller, and sold again for less, often with a warranty.
refurbished.example: A refurbished laptop for $780 instead of $1,100 new.

lessons.title: Unit Prices
lessons.summary: Compare packs of different sizes the right way.

steps.context: The [[unit price]] is the price for one unit (an ounce, a pound, a roll), so you can compare packs of different sizes.
steps.prompt: A 10 oz bag of rice costs $2.00. What’s the unit price?
A 24 oz jar of peanut butter costs $4.80. What’s the price per ounce?
Which pack is cheaper per roll?
What’s the big pack’s price per roll?
The bigger pack is always the better deal.
steps.explain: Usually, not always. Check the unit price, and only buy big if you’ll use it before it goes bad.

steps.prompt: When is the bigger pack a bad deal even though it’s cheaper per unit?
choices: When half of it goes bad before you use it
When it’s on the bottom shelf
steps.explain: Food you throw away has a unit price of “all of it.”

lessons.title: Cost per Use
lessons.summary: Why the pricier thing is sometimes the cheaper one.

steps.context: [[Cost per use]] is the price divided by how many times you’ll use something. A cheap thing used once can cost more per use than a pricey thing used every day.
steps.prompt: What does cost per use tell you?
choices: How much each use really costs
steps.explain: It spreads the price over every time you use the thing.

steps.prompt: Boots cost $120 and you’ll wear them about 300 times. What’s the cost per wear?
Cheaper boots cost $45 but fall apart after about 50 wears. Cost per wear?
Which boots are the better buy?
steps.explain: $0.40 a wear beats $0.90 a wear.

steps.prompt: A $60 outfit you’ll wear twice. Cost per wear?
A gym membership is $50 a month and you go 4 times a month. Cost per visit?
Cost per use only works for clothes.
steps.explain: Phones, tools, memberships: anything you use again and again.

lessons.title: Sale Tricks
lessons.summary: How stores make spending feel like saving.

steps.context: An [[anchor price]] is the big “was” price stores show so the sale price feels like a steal.
steps.prompt: “Was $200, now $99!” What does the $200 do?
choices: Makes $99 feel cheap, whether or not it is
Shows the store is losing money
steps.explain: The “was” price may never have been what anyone actually paid.

steps.prompt: If something is 50% off, buying it saves you money.
steps.explain: You only save if you’d have bought it anyway. Otherwise you spent 50%.

steps.prompt: Buy one, get one 50% off. Each shirt is $30. What do two cost?
You need one shirt. Is buy-one-get-one-50%-off a deal?
choices: Only if you’d really wear a second shirt
steps.explain: One shirt costs $30. Two cost $45. Only worth it if you wanted two.

steps.context: “Free shipping over $50” is designed to get you to add things.
steps.prompt: Your cart is $41 and shipping is $6. To get free shipping over $50, you add a $14 item you don’t need. How much more did you spend than if you’d paid shipping?
steps.explain: $14 − $6 = $8 more, for something you didn’t want.

steps.prompt: Real deal or trick?
items: Lower unit price on something you use every week
Adding items to reach free shipping
Sale on a winter coat you already planned to buy
“Was $300” on something that never sold for $300

lessons.title: Impulse Buys
lessons.summary: Wait a day. Most wants wear off.

steps.context: An [[impulse buy]] is something you buy on the spot, unplanned, because it grabbed you in the moment.
steps.prompt: Which is an impulse buy?
choices: Candy at the checkout that wasn’t on your list
steps.explain: Unplanned, grabbed in the moment: that’s an impulse buy.

steps.context: The 24-hour rule: if it isn’t a need and wasn’t planned, wait a day. If you still want it tomorrow, it might be worth it.
steps.prompt: You see $80 sneakers you love. What does the 24-hour rule say?
steps.explain: If you still want them tomorrow, they might be worth it.

steps.prompt: You make about 6 impulse buys a month at $15 each. What’s that in a year?
Saved card details and one-click checkout make impulse buys easier.
steps.explain: Every step removed is one less moment to think.

steps.prompt: Which trick cuts impulse buys the most?
choices: Removing saved cards and waiting a day
steps.explain: A little friction gives your brain time to catch up.

steps.prompt: Something catches your eye online. Put the smart steps in order.
items: Add it to a wish list instead of the cart
Check if it fits your budget
Buy it, or let it go
steps.explain: Park it, wait, check, decide.

lessons.title: Check the Receipt
lessons.summary: Scanners make mistakes. Catch them before you leave.

steps.context: Prices on the shelf and prices at the register don’t always match.
steps.prompt: The shelf tag said the yogurt was $3.49. Tap the line that’s wrong.
steps.explain: It rang up at $4.99, not $3.49.

steps.prompt: How much were you overcharged?
You ordered a large latte with oat milk and a muffin. Tap the charge you didn’t ask for.
steps.explain: Nobody asked for the extra shot.

steps.prompt: Stores sometimes scan the wrong price, so checking your receipt is worth the ten seconds.
steps.explain: Especially on sale items, where the shelf and the register often disagree.

steps.prompt: You spot a mistake after leaving the store. Best move?
choices: Go back or call with the receipt
steps.explain: Most stores fix it on the spot, and some give you the item free.

steps.prompt: If you were overcharged $1.50 every week, what would that add up to over a year of 52 weeks?

lessons.title: What Else Could It Buy?
lessons.summary: Every yes is a no to something else.

steps.context: [[Opportunity cost]] is what you give up when you choose one thing over another.
steps.prompt: You spend $60 on a new game. What’s the opportunity cost?
choices: Whatever else that $60 could have done, like going into savings
steps.explain: Not that the game was bad. Just that the $60 can’t do anything else now.

steps.prompt: A $6 lunch out every workday, about 20 days a month. What’s that a month?
And over a year?
Making lunch costs about $2. Over a year, how much more does buying lunch cost than making it?
Thinking about opportunity cost means never buying anything fun.
steps.explain: It means choosing on purpose. Buy the fun thing, knowing what it cost.

steps.prompt: Which question captures opportunity cost?
choices: What else could this money do?
steps.explain: Ask it before any purchase that isn’t a need.

lessons.title: Big Purchase, Smart Way
lessons.summary: New vs. refurbished, add-ons and “only $70 a month.”

steps.context: A [[refurbished]] item was returned or used, then checked and repaired by the seller. It often comes with a warranty and costs much less.
steps.prompt: Same model, both with a 1-year warranty. Which is the better deal?
steps.explain: Same machine, same warranty, $320 less.

steps.prompt: How much does the refurbished one save?

steps.context: Store protection plans often cost a lot for problems that rarely happen.
steps.prompt: The store offers a $150 “protection plan” on the $780 laptop. What should you check first?
choices: What it covers that the free warranty doesn’t
steps.explain: Many plans repeat what the warranty already covers.

steps.context: Monthly payments can hide extra cost. Always add it all up.
steps.prompt: “Only $70 a month for 12 months!” What’s the total?
Compared with paying $780 upfront, how much extra is that?
Before a big purchase, put these steps in order.
items: Decide what you need it to do
Check the total cost, not the monthly price
steps.explain: Need, compare, total, wait.

lessons.title: Taylor’s Shopping Trip
lessons.summary: One errand, four purchases. Work out what happened.

story.title: The $40 errand
story.body:
Taylor went to the store for one thing: a **$40** pair of work gloves.

Near the entrance, a speaker was marked “Was $120, now **$69**!” Taylor grabbed it. At checkout there was a buy-one-get-one-50%-off deal on **$12** phone chargers, so Taylor took two. A **$3** pack of gum went in at the register.

Taylor already owned a speaker and one working charger.

steps.prompt: How much did the two chargers cost?
What was Taylor’s total bill?
Taylor planned to spend $40. How far over plan was the trip?
Planned or impulse?
What made the speaker feel like a deal?
choices: The store was out of gloves
steps.explain: The anchor did the selling.

steps.prompt: Taylor can return the speaker within 30 days. Smart move?
choices: Return it: Taylor already has one
Buy a second one while it’s cheap
steps.explain: A $69 refund turns a $90 overspend into $21.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Smart Spending
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: 16 oz costs $3.20. 40 oz costs $7.20. What’s the 40 oz price per ounce?
steps.explain: $7.20 ÷ 40 = $0.18 an ounce, cheaper than $0.20.

steps.prompt: “Was $90, now $45.” What’s the $90?
steps.explain: It’s there to make $45 feel small.

steps.prompt: Cost per use can make a pricier item the cheaper choice.
steps.explain: If it lasts much longer, yes.

steps.prompt: $9 a day on snacks for 20 workdays. What’s that a month?
